title: Pharaoh's dreams (Genesis 41:1–40)
hookLine: seven fat cows, seven thin; Joseph plans for famine

cards: Two full years go by. Then the most powerful man in Egypt has a bad night. Pharaoh dreams he's standing by the Nile, and seven sleek, fat cows come up out of the river.
Then seven thin, ugly ones come up and eat the fat ones, and look just as thin as before. He sleeps again and dreams of seven full ears of grain on one stalk, swallowed by seven thin, scorched ones.
In the morning he calls every wise man and magician in Egypt. Nobody can tell him what it means. And the butler, holding the cup, suddenly remembers something.

teach.b: The butler confesses: I remember my faults this day. There was a young Hebrew in prison. Pharaoh sends for Joseph at once, and Joseph shaves and changes his clothes.
The young man who keeps losing his garments gets a new one. Pharaoh says, I hear you can interpret dreams.

teach.h: IT IS NOT IN ME: GOD WILL ANSWER.
teach.b: Joseph answers, in the King James Bible: "It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace." The same move as in prison: not me, God. The two dreams are one.

Seven good years of harvest are coming, then seven years of famine so severe the good years will be forgotten. The dream came twice, he says, because God has settled it. But Joseph doesn't stop at explaining.
He gives a plan. Set a wise man over the land.

teach.h: STORE A FIFTH FOR THE FAMINE.
teach.b: In the seven good years, store up a fifth of the harvest in the cities, kept for the famine. Don't spend all of the good years in the good years.

teach.h: A MAN IN WHOM THE SPIRIT OF GOD IS.
teach.b: Pharaoh asks his court: "Can we find such a one as this is, a man in whom the Spirit of God is?" And he puts Joseph over all Egypt, second only to Pharaoh.

This morning a forgotten prisoner; by the afternoon, he runs the country. Christians have read Joseph as a model of faith joined to practical wisdom: he trusts God with the future and still builds the barns.
Here, giving God the credit and drawing up a grain plan sit side by side.

how: Christians often point to Joseph's storehouses when teaching about stewardship and wise planning, and many church food banks and savings programs draw on this story.

a promise that the Nile would never run dry
a vision that Egypt would win a coming war

games.q: you're Joseph, just out of prison, standing before Pharaoh. you've explained the dreams: seven good years, seven of famine. what do you do next?
o: bow and wait to be sent back to prison.
propose a plan to store grain in the good years.
ask Pharaoh to set you free as payment.
games.why: he proposes a plan: a wise man over the land, a fifth of the harvest stored. Pharaoh gives the job to Joseph.

practice: Your fat years might be money, or energy, or time with someone who won't always be around; a lean season will likely come too: a hard stretch, a quiet one, getting older.
Picture one small thing you could set aside now: money, yes, but also patience, friendship, rest. If you pray, you can ask for wisdom about it.

wordCard.voice: Pharaoh's dreams. Seven fat cows and seven thin, seven full ears and seven scorched: seven years of plenty, then seven of famine.

orig.note: Hebrew spelling of Pharaoh, from an Egyptian phrase meaning great house, first the palace, then the king.
